The air hung heavy with the scent of rain-soaked earth, a rich, loamy fragrance that seeped into Lena’s skin as she stood on the patio, her fingers tracing the rough, weathered wood of the railing. The late afternoon sun, a reluctant orb behind a curtain of slate-gray clouds, cast a muted light over the garden, where droplets glistened on the petals of the peonies, each one a fragile promise of color against the encroaching gloom. She could taste the dampness on her lips, a sharp reminder of the storm that had swept through only moments before, leaving the world feeling fresh yet uncertain.

“Looks like we’re in for another one,” her brother Mark said, stepping outside, his voice breaking through the contemplative silence. He leaned against the doorframe, arms crossed, a half-smile tugging at the corners of his mouth. “You should probably put the cushions back in the shed.”

Lena glanced at the scattered outdoor cushions, their bright patterns stark against the darkened stones of the patio. “I’ll get to it,” she replied, her tone lighter than the weight in her chest suggested. She could feel the energy crackling in the air, a tension that mirrored the storm clouds above. “But I wanted to watch the rain first.”

Mark raised an eyebrow, a playful challenge dancing in his gaze. “Always the poet, aren’t you? It’s just rain.”

“Just rain?” She laughed, the sound surprising even herself, a burst of warmth in the chill of the impending downpour. “Have you ever stood in the middle of a storm and felt like the world was resetting itself?”

He shrugged, his posture relaxing, but the glint in his eyes remained skeptical. “I’m more of a ‘get out of the rain’ kind of guy.”
